absent: Full field layouts, sizes, and offsets of host CPU context, stage-2 MMU, vCPU, protected VM and vCPU, init params, and hypervisor page-table objects.
Numeric encodings and values of TLB operations, barriers, HCR, TCR, SCTLR, GIC, list-register, and page-table protection constants.
Validation, error handling, and allowed ranges for level, IPA, page count, handle, and address-width inputs beyond alignment and unknown-handle no-op.
Concurrency, reentrancy, and lock ordering for TLB maintenance beyond the page-table lock and VHE interrupt save and restore.
Contents, lifetime, and failure recovery for per-CPU windows, stacks, identity map, vectors, and host SVE mappings.
Range iteration details, stride adaptation, and hint selection beyond page-granular worst-case assumption.
Behavior of in-hypervisor helpers for stage-2 loading, TLB issue and sync, early allocation, VM lookup, and interrupt control beyond call sites shown.

findings.text: Host to hypervisor dispatch shims fetch a stage-2 MMU pointer plus address or level or range arguments from numbered host registers, translate the MMU pointer into hypervisor address space, and invoke the matching in-hypervisor TLB routine. The shims cover single IPA, non-shareable single IPA, address range, whole VMID, and local CPU context operations.

Per-address flush for a given VMID and translation level invalidates the stage-2 entry for that IPA and then the entire stage-1 EL1 TLB. It brackets the sequence with entry and exit of the target VMID context and orders the two invalidations so another CPU cannot refill a combined walk from stale stage-2 after stage-1 was cleared, followed by synchronization and instruction barrier.

Non-shareable per-address flush provides the same logical effect as the shareable variant but uses non-shareable invalidation scope and non-shareable barriers, with an initial visibility barrier whose domain follows the caller shareability request.

Range flush normalizes its start downward to page granularity and assumes worst-case page-sized mapping level, then applies a stage-2 range invalidation with unknown hint before the same full stage-1 invalidation, barrier, synchronization and exit sequence used by single-address flushes.

Whole-VMID flush invalidates both translation stages for the requested VMID in one combined operation while inside that VMID context, followed by hypervisor stage-1 synchronization and an instruction barrier before restoring the previous context.

Local CPU context flush invalidates the local stage-1 TLB and the entire instruction cache, ordered with non-shareable barriers and an instruction barrier, while inside the requested VMID context; it does not use shareable scope.

Non-VHE context switch first issues a visibility plus anti-speculation barrier, then fast-paths when already in the requested guest or host stage-2 context. Otherwise it records the outgoing MMU, optionally parks translation controls for the speculative address-translation workaround, loads the target stage-2, and guarantees exactly one instruction barrier. Exit reloads the saved MMU if any, re-issues a barrier, and restores parked controls.

VHE context switch saves interrupt state, records the outgoing vCPU stage-2 only when it differs, optionally parks translation controls for the speculative workaround, loads the requested stage-2, clears the TGE control so TLB operations affect guest EL1 and EL0 rather than host EL2 and EL0, and barriers. Exit restores host HCR flags, reloads any saved stage-2, restores parked controls, and restores interrupts.

All IPA and range flushes require stage-2 completion before stage-1 invalidation: a shareability-matched data barrier separates them, and a final synchronization plus instruction barrier follows the stage-1 invalidation. VHE additionally issues a store-visibility barrier before entering the target context.

On CPUs reporting the speculative address-translation erratum, context entry disables table-walk refills by setting table-control exclusion bits and ensuring stage-1 enable, preserving prior control values; exit conditionally restores them only when they were changed, avoiding stale walks with mismatched VMID.

Context entry expects to be invoked from vCPU run context when a running vCPU is present so the running-vCPU marker is valid; non-VHE signals an unexpected condition when the requested MMU is neither the running vCPU hardware MMU nor the host stage-2 MMU.

Protected VM whole-VMID dispatch resolves a VM reference from an opaque handle supplied by the host, does nothing when the handle is unknown, otherwise flushes that VM stage-2 MMU and releases the reference.

Timer offset dispatch copies the host-supplied 64-bit value into the virtual-counter offset system register for the current execution context; both VHE and non-VHE hypervisor variants expose the same effect.
Speculative store bypass safe dispatch reads the EL2 system control register, sets the control bit that forces safe speculation behavior, and writes the result back, leaving other bits unchanged.

GIC configuration probe determines whether a memory-mapped CPU interface is present by saving the system-register enable state, forcing that enable off under interrupt protection, reading back whether disable persisted, restoring the saved state, and reporting presence when the read-back shows disabled. VHE protects with interrupt masking while non-VHE toggles host interrupt overrides around the probe.

The GIC enable probe must prevent interrupt delivery while system-register access is disabled, because an interrupt in that window is unsafe; the two hypervisor modes use different masking mechanisms but both restore the prior mask and the saved enable value with barriers.
List-register initialization clears every virtual interrupt list register from zero through the maximum index decoded from the virtualization control register, leaving all entries zeroed.

Save and restore shims for interrupt priority and control state first resolve host and optional protected vCPU pointers and do nothing when host resolution fails. Direct path operates on host state only; protected path copies control plus all priority groups between host and hypervisor copies before or after invoking the in-hypervisor save or restore, with restore also installing a fixed system-register enable value on the hypervisor copy.

Protected hypervisor initialization dispatch forwards donated physical base, size, per-CPU base array, and address width to the bootstrap routine and returns its error code to the host; on success the bootstrap never returns normally but continues through an identity-map trampoline into finalization.

Bootstrap requires both donated base and size to be page aligned and validates the protected system-register table before touching memory; misaligned input fails immediately without further side effects.

Early memory division initializes the early allocator over the donated region then carves contiguous areas in fixed order for self-test, hypervisor vmemmap descriptors, VM table, hypervisor stage-1 tables, host stage-2 tables, and forwarding proxy state, failing with out-of-memory if any required carve-out cannot be satisfied.

Hypervisor page-table rebuild creates a fresh table with the early allocator, then installs identity map, vectors, vmemmap backing, executable and data and read-only and zero-initialized hypervisor sections, the whole donated pool, each CPU hypervisor per-CPU window and stack with recorded hypervisor address, and host vector state, aborting on first mapping failure.

Hypervisor page-table creation is serialized by a dedicated hypervisor spin lock: both the range-mapping helper and the low-level physical-to-virtual mapping helper acquire it around table updates and release it afterwards, with callers not required to hold it.

Vmemmap backing walks the recorded hypervisor memory blocks, aligns each block descriptor span to page boundaries, skips any prefix already covered by the previous block to avoid double mapping, maps backing pages for the remainder, zeroes the newly backed window, and advances the backing cursor; it succeeds trivially when a block yields an empty span.

TLB invalidation context is a small per-operation record holding the saved outgoing stage-2 MMU or null for no switch, plus saved translation and control registers for the erratum path and, on VHE, saved interrupt flags. Entry initializes it and exit consumes it to restore prior state.
